content:
I think you should take the job — but not as an escape, and not as a punishment. I think you should move toward a life where you are not just “the eldest daughter” by default, while also not treating your family as the enemy. The problem is not that you care about your parents. The problem is that the expectation has become a one-way street: your brother gets freedom, you get responsibility.

Your Swiss colleagues are right in one important sense: an expectation like that is oppressive if it is enforced by guilt, gender, birth order, and silence. But “just move out” is too blunt. Your mother crying is not proof that you are selfish. It is proof that this expectation is emotionally loaded — she may be afraid of being alone, of getting old, of losing control, of being a burden, or of you becoming distant. You can take that seriously without letting it make your decision for you.

If I were in your place, I would not stay only because they expect it. Staying out of duty can slowly turn into resentment, and resentment is a terrible foundation for long-term care. If you spend the next decade feeling trapped, you may end up caring for them out of obligation while your own life withers. That is not a good future for you, and it will not make you a better daughter.

But I would also not move in a way that says, “You were wrong, I am leaving you.” That can harden things, and it may make it harder for you to actually stay connected and involved later.

So I would do this: take the job if it gives you financial independence, a clearer future, and your own adult life — but frame the move as part of a caregiving plan, not a rejection of your parents.

You can say something like: “I am not abandoning you. I am taking this job because I need to build a stable life for myself. I will still be your daughter. I will visit/call regularly, and I will help with whatever is needed. But I cannot live my whole adult life as your default carer. We need to make a plan together, and I need you to support me in this.”

That sentence matters: “we need to make a plan together.” It shifts the issue from “may I go?” to “how will we care for everyone, including you, in a realistic way?” You are not asking permission to be a person. You are telling them what you are doing and asking them to participate in the consequences.

And yes, the brother should be part of that plan. Not because he has to become the main carer, but because the old script — “he lives his life, she manages the family” — cannot continue unchanged. If he is protected from responsibility, then you are being quietly taxed for the whole family.

There is also something important about the tears. When your mother cries, you do not have to collapse and say, “Fine, I’ll stay.” You can say, “I see that this hurts you. I’m sorry it hurts you. I love you. And I still need to go.” Tears can be grief. Tears can be love. Tears can also be pressure. You can honor the pain without accepting the demand.

I think the most adult thing you can do is stop treating this as “duty versus freedom.” The real question is: *Can you love your parents well from a place where you still have a life of your own?* If you stay and disappear into the role, you may become bitter. If you go and build yourself up, you may become someone who can actually help them later — financially, practically, emotionally — without disappearing.

So my honest answer is: go, if the job is a real step toward the life you want. But go with tenderness, clarity, and a plan. Do not make it a clean break. Do not make it a moral statement. Make it a transition.

You can be a good daughter and still leave the house. You can care for your parents and still refuse to be the only person who does. You can love your family and protect your future at the same time.
